questions.key_step: Sign-change conditions f(0)f(2)<0 and f(2)f(3)<0, then count integers.
questions.justification: Routine chain: two sign conditions, two quadratic inequalities, intersection and a count; no insight needed but the c-5 coefficient and endpoints need care.

questions.key_step: lambda+1/lambda=1 turns into (sum)^2 = 3 x product.
questions.justification: Symmetric-function condition on the ratio of roots, then a quadratic in m; the complex-ratio subtlety is only a consistency check.

questions.key_step: Sum 3/(m^2+1) is greatest at m=0.
questions.justification: One observation, then (a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2) with known sum and product.

questions.key_step: 1/alpha^12+1/beta^12 = (alpha^12+beta^12)/(alpha beta)^12.
questions.justification: Simplification is short but needs the reciprocal-power trick and (alpha-beta)^2 = sin(sin+8); chain of three routine steps.

questions.key_step: GP gives beta^2=alpha gamma, so first equation has equal roots -beta/alpha.
questions.justification: Three linked routine facts (GP, zero discriminant, root substitution) leading to gamma=alpha+beta.
One well-known recurrence applied to compute p1..p5 and check options.

questions.key_step: Repeated root gives b^2=5a; common root gives a=1/4.
questions.justification: Two root conditions combined and solved for a, b, then a symmetric function.

questions.key_step: Write f=k(x-3)(x-alpha) and use f(2)+f(-1)=0.
questions.justification: One substitution and a linear equation.

questions.key_step: Pair alpha+1/beta with beta+1/alpha and alpha-1/alpha with beta-1/beta.
questions.justification: Four-factor symmetric expression regrouped into sum/product form; routine multi-step algebra.

questions.key_step: 4 alpha^2+2 alpha=1 gives 2 alpha^2 = 1/2 - alpha.
questions.justification: One substitution using the root equation.

questions.key_step: Quadratic positive for all x iff discriminant < 0.
questions.justification: Single standard condition then an integer in an interval.

questions.key_step: Self-similar continued fraction: x = 3 + 1/(4+1/x).
questions.justification: One familiar trick (self-similarity) then a quadratic.

questions.key_step: Substitute t = x+1/x and test |t| >= 2.
questions.justification: One reduction; both t-values have |t|<2.

questions.key_step: Eliminate lambda: subtract the two equations to get lambda=7 alpha.
questions.justification: Common-root elimination, solve for alpha, find beta, gamma and the new quadratic; several routine stages.

questions.key_step: Domain restriction and squaring twice: reject extraneous roots on every branch of the domain.
questions.justification: Irrational equation with a three-part domain; the divide-by-sqrt(x-3) step hides the branch x<=-3, so a hasty student loses or gains a root.

questions.key_step: Divide by t^2 for a reciprocal (palindromic-type) quartic; z = t-1/t.
questions.justification: Reciprocal-quartic substitution then positivity of t=e^x and sign of x.
Three sign conditions; one integer.

questions.key_step: Case split on the sign of (x-3)(x-5) and accept only roots inside each case.
questions.justification: Two cases, each quadratic, with acceptance checks; routine.

questions.key_step: Use alpha=-1, beta+gamma=1, beta gamma=1 so beta, gamma are -omega, -omega^2 (cubes = -1).
questions.justification: Vieta for a cubic plus cube roots of unity, a second chapter's idea but short.

questions.key_step: Polar form sqrt3 e^{+-3 i pi/4}: alpha^n+beta^n = 2*3^{n/2} cos(3 n pi/4), several terms vanish.
questions.justification: Needs polar form of complex roots and De Moivre with high powers, careful angle reduction; slip-prone with no way to check, though options help.
